title: Network Performance & QoS
summary: Numbers that tell you how healthy a network is — and how QoS keeps real-time traffic from suffering.

blocks.markdown:
**Network performance** describes how efficiently data moves between two points. Three core questions: How fast? How reliably? How consistently?

- **Bandwidth** — max capacity of the pipe.
- **Throughput** — what actually flows through it.
- **Latency** — how long each trip takes.
- **QoS** ensures critical traffic (voice, video) gets priority when the pipe is shared.

blocks.subTitle: Metric map
blocks.markdown:
Quick reference — six metrics you must know.

| Metric | What it measures |
|---|---|
| Bandwidth | Max bits/sec the link can carry |
| Throughput | Actual bits/sec delivered |
| Latency | One-way delay (sender → receiver) |
| RTT | Round-trip time (send + reply) |
| Jitter | Variation in latency between packets |
| Packet loss | % of packets that never arrive |

blocks.subTitle: Bandwidth vs throughput
blocks.markdown:
**Bandwidth** is the rated capacity of a link — the maximum it could carry (e.g., 1 Gbps fiber). **Throughput** is the actual data delivered per second, always ≤ bandwidth.

- Congestion, packet loss, and protocol overhead all shrink throughput.
- A 1 Gbps link with 30% loss delivers ~700 Mbps of useful data at best.

Bandwidth is potential; throughput is reality.

blocks.subTitle: Latency and RTT
blocks.markdown:
**Latency** is the one-way delay from sender to receiver. **RTT (Round-Trip Time)** is the time for a packet to travel there and back — what `ping` measures.

- RTT ≈ 2 × latency (roughly), but asymmetric paths make this imprecise.
- A 20 ms RTT feels snappy; 300 ms makes interactive apps sluggish.
- High latency does not mean high packet loss — they are independent.

blocks.subTitle: Jitter and packet loss
blocks.markdown:
**Jitter** is the variance in latency across consecutive packets. If packets arrive at 10 ms, 25 ms, 12 ms, the jitter is ~15 ms.

- High jitter breaks real-time audio — the playback engine can't predict when the next frame arrives.
- **Packet loss** is the percentage of packets that never reach the destination (dropped at congested routers or corrupted in transit).
- Even 1% loss causes audible glitches in VoIP and visible artifacts in video.

Latency has four additive components:

- **Propagation delay** — physical travel time at ~2/3 the speed of light. Fixed by distance; a London–Sydney link adds ~170 ms minimum.
- **Transmission delay** — time to push all bits onto the wire: packet size ÷ link bandwidth.
- **Queuing delay** — time spent waiting in a router's buffer behind other packets. Varies with congestion.
- **Processing delay** — time a router takes to inspect and forward a packet. Usually microseconds.

- Propagation dominates long-haul paths; queuing dominates congested links.
- Fixing one delay doesn't eliminate the others.

**Bandwidth-delay product (BDP)** = bandwidth × RTT. It tells you how many bytes are "in flight" at any moment.

- A 100 Mbps link with 100 ms RTT has BDP = 1.25 MB — the sender must have that much data outstanding to keep the link full.
- TCP's congestion window must be ≥ BDP to saturate a high-latency, high-bandwidth path.
- Also called the **pipe volume** — undersizing the window wastes capacity. See [congestion-control](congestion-control).

blocks.subTitle: What it is
blocks.markdown:
**QoS (Quality of Service)** is a set of mechanisms that control how a network handles different types of traffic — ensuring critical flows get the resources they need.

- Without QoS, all packets compete equally; a bulk file transfer can crowd out a video call on the same link.
- QoS mechanisms: **classification** (tag packets by type), **scheduling** (decide which to send first), **policing/shaping** (limit or smooth burst rates).
- Defined in standards like **DiffServ** (IP header DSCP field) and **IEEE 802.1p** (Ethernet frames).

blocks.subTitle: Traffic classes
blocks.markdown:
Traffic is classified into priority tiers.

| Class | Examples | Sensitivity |
|---|---|---|
| Real-time | VoIP, video conferencing | Latency + jitter |
| Interactive | Gaming, SSH | Latency |
| Bulk | File transfers, backups | Throughput only |

- Real-time traffic is sent first, even if it means bulk transfers wait.
- Starvation of low-priority flows is prevented by **minimum bandwidth guarantees**.

blocks.subTitle: Buffering trade-off
blocks.markdown:
**Buffering** absorbs bursts by queuing packets before they're forwarded. It sounds like a fix, but it introduces **bufferbloat** — excessive delay from over-large buffers.

- A router with a 500 ms buffer hides packet loss but adds ~500 ms of latency to every flow.
- Real-time apps can't tolerate it: a call with 500 ms delay sounds like a satellite phone.
- **AQM (Active Queue Management)** — e.g., CoDel — drops or marks packets early to keep buffers short and latency low.

Tools and levers for performance work:

- **Measure latency/RTT** — `ping`, `traceroute`; for per-path breakdown use `mtr`.
- **Measure throughput** — `iperf3` between endpoints.
- **Measure jitter/loss** — streaming `iperf3` with UDP, or purpose-built probes.
- **Improve**: reduce hops, move servers closer (see [cdn-edge-caching](cdn-edge-caching)), tune TCP buffers to match BDP, enable QoS, fix congestion (see [network-reliability-observability](network-reliability-observability)).

blocks.subTitle: Bandwidth vs throughput vs latency
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is the difference between bandwidth, throughput, and latency?**

**Bandwidth** is the link's rated capacity (max possible). **Throughput** is actual data delivered — always ≤ bandwidth, reduced by loss and overhead. **Latency** is the per-packet delay and is independent of bandwidth; a high-bandwidth link can still have high latency (e.g., satellite).

Think: bandwidth is the pipe width, throughput is how much water flows, latency is how long a single drop takes to arrive.

blocks.subTitle: What is jitter and why does it matter
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is jitter and why does it matter for real-time applications?**

**Jitter** is the variation in packet arrival delay. If packets arrive every 20 ms on average but swing ±15 ms, the receiver can't play them back smoothly.

Real-time apps use a **jitter buffer** to absorb the variance — but a large buffer adds latency. VoIP targets < 30 ms jitter; above ~50 ms calls degrade noticeably.

blocks.subTitle: Components of latency
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What are the four components of latency?**

1. **Propagation** — distance / (2/3 × speed of light). Irreducible for a given path.
2. **Transmission** — packet size ÷ link rate. Reduce by sending smaller packets.
3. **Queuing** — wait behind other packets. Reduce with QoS and AQM.
4. **Processing** — router forwarding overhead. Usually negligible.

Propagation sets the floor; queuing is where most optimization happens.
